extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, especially those studying Schopenhauer, metaphysics, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository philosophical treatment of ethics and metaphysics arguing that the 'denial of the will' (via a changed form of knowledge) is the path to salvation; discusses suicide, asceticism, freedom, Christian doctrine parallels, and the metaphysical consequence that abolition of will abolishes the world as idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence of the will requires knowledge, not physical force
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It itself can never be transcended except through knowledge. Thus the only way of salvation is, that the will shall manifest itself unrestrictedly ... Only as the result of this knowledge can the will transcend itself,’ and physical means (destroying the germ, killing the child, suicide) cannot accomplish transcendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical destruction affects only the manifestation at a place and time; the will-as-thing-in-itself can only be overcome when its manifestation attains self-knowledge. ‘Nature guides the will to the light, just because it is only in the light that it can work out its salvation.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascetic starvation as a distinct form of self-denial (not despair-suicide)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This kind of suicide is so far from being the result of the will to live, that such a completely resigned ascetic only ceases to live because he has already altogether ceased to will.’ Starvation voluntarily chosen on grounds of extreme asceticism differs from common suicide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical case reports and medical/journal references are cited; instances are often obscured by religious fanaticism or insanity labels. Only death by starvation fits the pure form, since an intention to escape torment would re-assert will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom belongs to the will-in-itself; manifestation obeys necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Real freedom, i.e., independence of the principle of sufficient reason, belongs to the will only as a thing-in-itself, not to its manifestation, whose essential form is everywhere the principle of sufficient reason…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manifestation can show freedom only in the unique case when it makes an end of what manifests itself (e.g., organs of generation present but no sensual gratification desired). Thus freedom appears in the denial/abolition of the character manifested by motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-suppression of character proceeds from a changed form of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The state in which the character is withdrawn from the power of motives does not proceed directly from the will, but from a changed form of knowledge.’ When the principium individuationis is seen through and the inner nature (Ideas) recognised, motives lose effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because knowledge is involuntary, the entrance into this freedom (denial of will) cannot be achieved by intention or design but comes suddenly and from within; the Church rightly calls it 'the work of grace' or 'new birth'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian dogmas symbolise assertion and denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian theology symbolises 'nature' as the assertion of the will to live in Adam (original sin) and 'grace' as the denial of the will (salvation) in the incarnate God; Jesus should be conceived as the symbol/personification of the denial of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dogmas, while foreign in form to philosophy, correspond in essence to the ethical doctrine developed: assertion of the will (sin, suffering) versus denial (salvation), and the Church's language (work of grace, new birth) maps onto Schopenhauer's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good works (motive-driven action) cannot justify; salvation is through faith (changed knowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If it were works, which spring from motives and deliberate intention, that led to salvation ... virtue would always be a prudent, methodical, far-seeing egoism.’ Salvation is through faith, i.e., through a changed mode of knowing, which comes by grace from without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works remain as fruits or symptoms of faith but cannot themselves constitute merit or justification because they are intentional actions induced by motives (opus operatum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom requires deliberative reason; animals lack freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The possibility of the freedom which thus expresses itself is the greatest prerogative of man, which is for ever wanting to the brute, because the condition of it is the deliberation of reason... The brute is entirely without the possibility of freedom.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom arises from the capacity to survey life independently of present impressions (abstract ideas); brutes act with necessity like stones or wolves, lacking this deliberative faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity (kingdom of Nature) vs Freedom (kingdom of Grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise normative dichotomy: ‘Necessity is the kingdom of nature; freedom is the kingdom of grace.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity governs all manifestations bound by the principle of sufficient reason (motives, character). Freedom is the exceptional result of the will-in-itself denying its manifested character via changed knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of the will entails the abolition of the world as idea
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘With the free denial, the surrender of the will, all those phenomena are also abolished ... the whole manifestation of the will; and, finally, also the universal forms of this manifestation, time and space, and also its last fundamental form, subject and object; all are abolished. No will: no idea, no world.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The denial of will is metaphysically radical: since the world-as-idea is the objectivity/mirror of will, abolishing will removes the world’s objectivity (it 'vanishes into nothing' for those still ensnared by willing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing is relative (nihil privativum) — absolute nothing is unthinkable
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘No absolute nothing, no proper nihil negativum is even thinkable; but everything of this kind ... is always merely a nihil privativum. Every nothing is thought as such only in relation to something, and presupposes this relation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to posit a positive knowledge of the denial-of-will must acknowledge that 'nothing' is always a negation of a definite something; the philosophical account stays at a negative description while mystical reports point to an experiential state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystical ecstasy is non-conceptual, experiential, and incommunicable (not proper propositional knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If ... a positive knowledge should be attained ... there would be nothing for it but to refer to that state ... denoted by ecstasy, rapture, illumination, union with God ... a state, however, which cannot properly be called knowledge, because it has not the form of subject and object, and is, moreover, only attainable in one’s own experience and cannot be further communicated.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must remain with negative conceptual description; mystical states provide phenomenological affirmation but are not transmittable propositional knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenological fruits of denial: peace, calm, and serenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of the will results in 'peace which is above all reason, that perfect calm of the spirit, that deep rest, that inviolable confidence and serenity' perceptible in saints and represented in art (Raphael, Correggio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemplation of such lives and representations offers consolation against the dread of 'nothingness' after abolition of will; the state leaves 'only knowledge' once the will has vanished.
